newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia landslide surviver thanks rescuers.
newsitem.headline: Australia landslide surviver thanks rescuers.

text.p: The survivor of Australia's ski-village landslide on Sunday paid tribute from his hospital bed to the exhausted search crews still tunnelling into rubble for 10 people still missing.
Ski instructor Stuart Diver, who answered prayers for a miracle on Saturday when he emerged from 64 hours trapped in the wreckage of two collapsed ski lodges, said he felt overwhelmed.
Propped up on pillows, Diver, 27, showed no sign of his three-day ordeal trapped in a concrete tomb.
"I'd just like to thank everyone who was involved in my rescue...," he said in a clear, normal voice.
"It's been overwhelming and I don't think I'd have made it through without the involvement of all those people. It's been fantastic, and thanks very much."

Diver's wife, Sally, is among the 19 other people entombed in a mass of broken concrete, twisted metal, dirt and splintered trees when a steep, heavily developed hillside at the Thredbo ski village, southwest of Sydney, suddenly gave way.
The couple were in bed together when disaster struck.
Rescuers on Sunday brought sniffer dogs onto the scene to help look for more survivors, but they failed to find any more than the nine dead bodies which had already been discovered.
Eight have been recovered. Police would not identify them.
Police said the chance of finding another survivor was slim, but a firefighter said it was likely other air pockets, like the one that entombed Diver, existed.

Rescuers continued to burrow beneath big concrete slabs thought to have come to rest on many of the victims, inching their way through the dangerously unstable rubble. About 24 metres (85 ft) of tunnelling now snakes through the debris.
Floor plans of the lodges are being used to target bedrooms which, due to the late hour of the disaster on Wednesday night, are believed to hide many of the missing victims.

"The rescue teams will not give up hope of finding other people alive until we have accounted for every single person trapped in that rubble," police superintendent Charlie Sanderson told reporters as another freezing night fell on the site.
Temperatures have plunged to as low as minus 12 degrees Celsius (10 Fahrenheit).
In warmer climates, victims of building collapses have survived for over a week, especially if water is present.

In South Korea last year, a woman trapped with food and water survived for 16 days in a collapsed department store. In 1990, a woman was pulled alive from debris 13 days after one of China's worst recorded earthquakes.
But while rescuers hope for another miracle, the constant reminder of death is ever present at the Thredbo landslide.
Rescuers found two more bodies overnight and another on Sunday, bringing the death toll to nine.
Wearing face masks against the stifling smell, rescuers recovered four more bodies from the rubble on Sunday, bringing to eight the number of victims recovered. One body has yet to be freed.

Diver has told rescuers of his amazing survival and how he desperately tried to save his wife. As underground water filled the cavity in which he and his wife were trapped, he tried to hold his wife's head above water.
But Sally was pinned on a mattress beside him by something heavy and a sudden rush of water ripped her from his grip.
Diver is recovering in a hospital in Canberra, 150 km (90 miles) north of Thredbo, where he is expected to remain for a few days.
"I continued to hope there would be a miracle and there was," Diver's father, Steve, told reporters in Canberra.
"I spoke to him by phone (held by rescuers) when he was still in the hole just to say hello and tell him we were with him."
A memorial service, attended by family and friends of the victims as well as acting Prime Minister Tim Fischer, will be held at Thredbo's small ecumenical church on Monday.

A fund was set up on Sunday for people who lost loved ones in the landslide. Thredbo Alpine Village, a resort company, said it would donate a tenth of its revenue for the rest of winter to the fund. It estimated this would amount to about A$1 million.
